title: Defence at 3% of GDP from April 2027
headline: Bring the 3% forward from 2030-31. About £4.2bn in 2029-30, falling.
description: The government has committed to 3% of GDP on defence in the next Parliament and 3.5% by 2035, and the OBR's forecast already has defence rising from 2.4% of GDP in 2025-26 to 3.0% by 2030-31. This card gets there from April 2027 instead. The cost is the gap between 3% and the OBR's path, multiplied by nominal GDP: about £11.8bn in 2027-28, £8.1bn in 2028-29, £4.2bn in 2029-30 and nothing in 2030-31, when the path arrives on its own. The years between the OBR's two published points are filled in by straight line, which is our assumption.

baselinePolicy.text: The OBR assumes defence spending rises from 2.4% of GDP in 2025-26 to 3.0% by 2030-31, on the way to the Government's commitment of 3.5% by 2035; the Defence Investment Plan's explainer says 3% in the next Parliament.

source.quote: spending on defence rises from 2.4 per cent in 2025-26 to 3.0 per cent by the end of the forecast

alreadyIncludes: Defence RDEL of £42.0bn and CDEL of £31.5bn in 2028-29 (Spending Review 2025, Tables 5.3 and 5.4).
The 3.5%-by-2035 commitment and 3% in the next Parliament (Defence Investment Plan funding explainer).

source.table: Paragraph 4.15 and the nominal GDP forecast

rawSource.note: The OBR publishes the two ends of the path, 2.4% in 2025-26 and 3.0% in 2030-31, not the years between. Those are filled in by straight-line interpolation, which is our assumption, not the OBR's. The cost is then (3% − that share) × nominal GDP, which reaches nought in 2030-31 because the forecast gets there anyway.

caveats: The OBR's path reaches 3% in 2030-31 on its own, so this buys the earlier years and nothing after: a front-loaded cost that falls to nought, not a permanent uplift.

The share is split 43% capital and 57% day-to-day, the split in the Spending Review's own defence settlement for 2028-29 (£31.5bn capital, £42.0bn resource). Capital spending does not count against the stability rule, so the split matters as much as the total.
Nobody has costed this timetable. The arithmetic is ours: a target share of GDP against a straight line between the OBR's two published points.

considerations.text: The forecast already climbs to 3% by 2030-31 and the Defence Investment Plan says 3% in the next Parliament; bringing it forward is a question of years, not of the destination. The Spending Review counts NATO-qualifying spending, which reaches 2.6% of GDP by 2027 and includes part of the intelligence budget; the OBR counts defence spending, 2.4% in 2025-26; the two are not the same measure.

sources.note: 3% in the next Parliament; 3.5% of GDP by 2035

considerations.text: The OBR already notes that meeting existing commitments leaves unprotected day-to-day spending falling 4.4% a year in real terms at the end of the forecast. Extra defence spending inside a fixed envelope would have to come from somewhere else, or from borrowing.

sources.quote: falling by 4.4 per cent a year in real terms in the final two years of the forecast

considerations.text: Whether defence could spend an extra £11.8bn well in 2027-28 is a question about industry, procurement and recruitment, not the public finances; the Defence Investment Plan's own funding is set over four years for that reason.

interactions.text: Both raise defence: the day-to-day slider moves the Spending Review settlement, this one buys the path to 3% of GDP, and the two add up.
The £4.7bn the plan's explainer still has to find is part of getting to 3%; funding both counts some of the same money twice.
